extracted.intended_audience: aspiring flash-fiction writers / fiction writers new to very-short forms
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing effective flash fiction—complete short stories of ~1,000 words or less (including micro- and nano-fiction variants) that create emotional impact and narrative satisfaction within severe length constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length / definition (flash, micro, nano)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash fiction is a story in 1,000 words or less. Micro fiction is under 500 words; nano fiction is under 100 words (and pieces as short as six words exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a strict working constraint for the form; choose the sub-form you want to write to and respect the brevity. Remember titles do not count toward the word limit (see Creative Title).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Just like any narrative, flash fiction needs a beginning, middle, and end. A clear story goal, a.k.a. plot. Well-developed hero and villain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of length you cannot have subplots — focus on one plot and one main conflict that needs to appear pretty much immediately. Limit scene changes and POV switches; only use them if they truly enhance the story. Keep the structure tight so every beat advances the story toward resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hook (opening sentence importance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In flash fiction the hook is often the opening sentence—it should set the tone, introduce your character, and give an inkling of the main conflict (or dive right into it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You have very little space to grab and keep the reader; treat the first line as the primary hook. If a reader puts down the piece early, it’s likely doomed, so craft an opening that immediately engages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension (forward momentum in every line)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tension is the ‘what’s going to happen next’ factor. In flash there needs to be tension in every sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each sentence moves the story forward and raises stakes or questions. Imagine crafting the story so every line creates expectation or unease that propels the reader toward the ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tight writing (every word counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every word counts in flash fiction; use words effectively to maintain brevity without sacrificing quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: backload sentences (put resonant words/phrases at the end), use dynamic/specific verbs instead of bland 'be' verbs, pick specific nouns (e.g., 'Volvo' instead of 'car'), use adjectives/adverbs sparingly and powerfully, avoid passive voice which often requires more words. Caveats: do not choose shortest phrasing if it forces telling instead of showing; do not overload with adverbs for the sake of concision. Preserve showing of action, emotion, and conflict even when compressing language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative title (subtext and double-meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles don’t count toward your word limit but should be concise, clever, and often carry double meaning or subtext.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the title to ground readers in context, hint at theme, or add resonance after reading (e.g., a title that is a red herring or that signals a retelling). Load the title with subtext when possible to deepen the story without using words from the main text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting (specific, evocative, can act as character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even with limited words, readers need a sense of place and time; setting can and should carry subtext.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose deliberate nouns and a few vivid details (e.g., 'vine crawling up a flagpole out of an abandoned playground’s crumbled asphalt') to evoke broad context. You can focus on a single evocative element of setting rather than trying to describe everything. Consider making setting function like a character to add depth without extra exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and POV (small cast, clear stakes)
rubrics_metrics.description: You need a clear hero and villain (or central opposing force); characters must feel real, not cardboard. Use a small cast and typically a single POV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit cast size so you have space to develop the protagonist and conflict. Choose the POV character who has the most to lose or the highest stakes. One POV is usually sufficient; unconventional POVs are possible but should be chosen deliberately (e.g., a snowflake).

rubrics_metrics.name: Backstory (show, don’t dump)
rubrics_metrics.description: Backstory exists but should not be dumped; necessary information must come out naturally and only as the reader needs to know it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid large expository blocks explaining past events. Weave needed context organically into present action and dialogue; flash forces efficient integration of backstory into the narrative flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional investment (show rather than tell)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great fiction connects emotionally; flash requires showing emotional experience rather than naming it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let readers feel emotion through sensory detail and action (e.g., use 'Harry gritted his teeth' rather than 'Harry gritted his teeth in determination'). Reserve explicit naming of emotion for rare, deliberate moments. Emotional resonance is crucial in limited space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twist (satisfying near-end revelation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A twist ending is common and often expected in flash fiction; it usually appears near the end and reframes the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up and veil the twist so that the payoff feels inevitable yet surprising—readers should be able to look back and say they should have seen it coming. The twist should make the ending hard-striking and satisfying, synthesizing the story’s clues and subtext.
